389: Springiness (Table 4.31 and Fig. 4.31) differed significantly among the twelve treatment combinations. It was highest in DI (1.04), followed by RI (1.02), and lowest in KBI (0.46). Among the products the mean value was 0.99 in the plain product, 0.73 in the carrot fortified product and 0.54 in the beet fortified product. Among the varieties it was highest in Radhunipagal (0.79) and lowest in Kalojira (0.69).
390: The variety and product interaction was significant, the critical difference at the 5 per cent level being 0.68, with a coefficient of variation of 4.40 per cent.
392: Springiness expresses the elastic recovery of the product following the first compression, and the most probable basis of its decline on fortification is the weakening of the amylose network providing that elasticity. The amylose liberated during steaming re-associates as the product cools and forms a continuous gel permitting the crumb to spring back, so that treatments of higher amylose content necessarily recover better (Tester et al., 2004; Mohapatra and Bal, 2006; Copeland et al., 2009). Since fortification lowered amylose, springiness declined with it, and the correlation between the two characters recorded in the present study supports this interpretation. The gas cell structure generated during fermentation likewise contributes to elastic recovery, and the dilution of the black gram protein stabilising those cells constitutes a second probable factor in the decline (Reddy et al., 1981; Nisha et al., 2005; Durgadevi and Shetty, 2012). Comparable relationships between springiness and starch structure have been reported for other steamed cereal products (Rosenthal, 1999; Bourne, 2002). A comparable decline in springiness on partial replacement of the rice component was recorded by Kaviyaselvan et al. (2026), who concluded that the cereal fraction contributes to this attribute alongside the black gram.
401: Cohesiveness (Table 4.32 and Fig. 4.32) differed significantly among the twelve treatment combinations. It was highest in KI (0.94), followed by GI (0.91), and lowest in KBI (0.40). Among the products the mean value was 0.85 in the plain product, 0.65 in the carrot fortified product and 0.54 in the beet fortified product. Among the varieties it was highest in Gobindabhog (0.78) and lowest in Dudeshwar (0.57).
402: The variety and product interaction was significant, the critical difference at the 5 per cent level being 0.04, with a coefficient of variation of 5.50 per cent.
404: Cohesiveness measures the strength of the internal bonds holding the product together, so that the most probable basis of its decline on fortification is the dilution of the starch and protein matrix supplying those bonds (Rosenthal, 1999; Bourne, 2002). The addition of a vegetable extract introduces fibre and moisture but no structural protein, so that the continuity of the matrix is interrupted and the crumb is more readily broken apart (Wilkinson et al., 2000; Sharma et al., 2012; Chhikara et al., 2019). The strong contribution of black gram protein to this property is well established, the globulin and arabinogalactan of black gram forming the film that binds the gas cell walls together (Reddy et al., 1981; Nisha et al., 2005; Durgadevi and Shetty, 2012). The retrograded amylose network provides a second binding mechanism, which accounts for the treatments richest in amylose proving also the most cohesive (Tester et al., 2004; Mohapatra and Bal, 2006).
413: Gumminess (Table 4.33 and Fig. 4.33) differed significantly among the twelve treatment combinations. It was highest in KI (11890.93), followed by GI (7980.59), and lowest in KBI (2164.66). Among the products the mean value was 7272.78 in the plain product, 3727.10 in the carrot fortified product and 3397.86 in the beet fortified product. Among the varieties it was highest in Gobindabhog (6053.10) and lowest in Dudeshwar (3446.84).
414: The variety and product interaction was significant, the critical difference at the 5 per cent level being 102.30, with a coefficient of variation of 1.84 per cent.
416: Gumminess is a secondary parameter computed as the product of hardness and cohesiveness, so that the most probable basis of its behaviour is simply that both of its components declined on fortification and the effect was consequently multiplied (Bourne, 2002; Szczesniak, 2002). Treatments both firm and strongly bound returned very high values, while treatments soft and weakly bound returned low ones. The underlying causes are those already discussed, namely the dilution of the black gram protein and rice starch network by the vegetable extract and the accompanying loss of amylose available for retrogradation (Reddy et al., 1981; Nisha et al., 2005; Tester et al., 2004; Durgadevi and Shetty, 2012). Since gumminess describes the energy required to disintegrate a semi-solid food to a state ready for swallowing, the lower values of the fortified treatments correspond to a product more readily eaten, consistent with their higher sensory texture scores (Rosenthal, 1999; Wilkinson et al., 2000). Kaviyaselvan et al. (2026) reported the same relationship in idli, gumminess and chewiness both declining when the rice component was partly replaced.
425: Chewiness (Table 4.34 and Fig. 4.34) differed significantly among the twelve treatment combinations. It was highest in KI (10263.60), followed by GI (6593.36), and lowest in KBI (945.13). Among the products the mean value was 6148.99 in the plain product, 2212.18 in the carrot fortified product and 1681.00 in the beet fortified product. Among the varieties it was highest in Kalojira (4364.63) and lowest in Dudeshwar (2049.58).
426: The variety and product interaction was significant, the critical difference at the 5 per cent level being 83.10, with a coefficient of variation of 2.14 per cent.
428: Chewiness is the product of gumminess and springiness and is therefore doubly dependent upon the primary texture parameters, which constitutes the most probable basis of the very wide range recorded (Bourne, 2002; Szczesniak, 2002). Treatments simultaneously hard, cohesive and elastic required the greatest work of mastication, and these were the plain products, in which the black gram protein and rice starch network was undiluted and the amylose content highest (Reddy et al., 1981; Nisha et al., 2005; Tester et al., 2004). The fortified treatments, in which all three primary parameters were lower, yielded a product breaking down rapidly in the mouth (Wilkinson et al., 2000; Durgadevi and Shetty, 2012). The close correspondence between these instrumental values and the texture scores awarded by the panel supports the position of Szczesniak (2002) and Rosenthal (1999) that instrumental texture profile analysis of a steamed cereal food reflects perceived texture reliably.
437: Resilience (Table 4.35 and Fig. 4.35) differed significantly among the twelve treatment combinations. It was highest in GI (0.55), followed by KI (0.48), and lowest in RBI (0.19). Among the products the mean value was 0.46 in the plain product, 0.27 in the carrot fortified product and 0.22 in the beet fortified product. Among the varieties it was highest in Gobindabhog (0.36) and lowest in Radhunipagal (0.27).
438: The variety and product interaction was significant, the critical difference at the 5 per cent level being 0.04, with a coefficient of variation of 11.71 per cent.
440: Resilience expresses the instantaneous elastic recovery of the product during the first compression and is therefore closely related to springiness, which constitutes the most probable basis of the two characters behaving alike (Rosenthal, 1999; Bourne, 2002). The recovery is contingent upon the elasticity of the retrograded amylose gel and of the protein films surrounding the gas cells, both of which were diluted by the vegetable extract (Reddy et al., 1981; Nisha et al., 2005; Tester et al., 2004). The comparatively high coefficient of variation recorded for this character is to be expected, since resilience is determined over a very short interval and is sensitive to small differences in the porosity of individual samples, a limitation noted for soft aerated foods generally (Wilkinson et al., 2000; Szczesniak, 2002; Durgadevi and Shetty, 2012). Kaviyaselvan et al. (2026) likewise found resilience to be conditioned by both cultivar and the composition of the product.
451: Aroma score (Table 4.36 and Fig. 4.36) differed significantly among the twelve treatment combinations. It was highest in GI (7.70), followed by GCI (7.25), and lowest in KCI (5.65). Among the products the mean value was 6.82 in the plain product, 6.40 in the beet fortified product and 6.24 in the carrot fortified product. Among the varieties it was highest in Gobindabhog (7.37) and lowest in Dudeshwar (5.83).
452: The variety and product interaction was significant, the critical difference at the 5 per cent level being 0.54, with a coefficient of variation of 7.14 per cent.
454: The most probable basis of the high aroma scores of the plain products of the aromatic landraces is that 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline, the principal volatile responsible for the characteristic aroma of scented rice, survives the entire preparation sequence of soaking, grinding, fermentation and steaming (Buttery et al., 1983; Bhattacharjee et al., 2002; Yoshihashi et al., 2002). Its retention under moist heat has been demonstrated repeatedly, so that the aroma of a scented landrace is expressed in cooked and processed products as well as in the grain itself (Wongpornchai et al., 2004; Champagne, 2008; Sakthivel et al., 2009). The lower scores of the fortified treatments within each aromatic variety are most probably attributable to sensory masking, the earthy geosmin of beetroot and the terpenes of carrot competing with the rice volatile for the attention of the panel rather than destroying it chemically (Sharma et al., 2012; Ghosh and Roychoudhury, 2018; Chhikara et al., 2019). A small loss through volatilisation during the protracted fermentation of the batter may contribute further (Blandino et al., 2003).
463: Taste score (Table 4.37 and Fig. 4.37) differed significantly among the twelve treatment combinations. It was highest in KBI (7.69), followed by RBI (7.29), and lowest in DI (5.16). Among the products the mean value was 7.11 in the beet fortified product, 6.76 in the carrot fortified product and 6.06 in the plain product. Among the varieties it was highest in Kalojira (7.23) and lowest in Dudeshwar (5.91).
464: The variety and product interaction was non-significant for this character.
466: The most probable basis of the improvement in taste on fortification is the free sugar contributed by the vegetable extract, beetroot and carrot both carrying appreciable quantities of sucrose and reducing sugars that sweeten the product perceptibly (Sharma et al., 2012; Singh and Hathan, 2014; Chhikara et al., 2019). The organic acids produced during lactic fermentation confer upon idli its characteristic mild sourness, and the added sweetness balances this acidity and improves the overall taste impression (Soni and Sandhu, 1990; Nout and Sarkar, 1999; Blandino et al., 2003). A second and less direct factor is that the visual appeal of a coloured product elevates the scores awarded for taste, a cross-modal interaction well documented in sensory evaluation (Amerine et al., 1965; Francis, 1995; Meilgaard et al., 2007). The non-significant interaction indicates that this gain was of equal magnitude in all four varieties, so that the effect is a property of the fortifying material rather than of any particular landrace (Pal et al., 2019).
475: Flavour score (Table 4.38 and Fig. 4.38) differed significantly among the twelve treatment combinations. It was highest in KBI (7.96), followed by RBI (7.56), and lowest in DI (5.46). Among the products the mean value was 7.38 in the beet fortified product, 7.13 in the carrot fortified product and 6.31 in the plain product. Among the varieties it was highest in Kalojira (7.50) and lowest in Dudeshwar (6.34).
476: The variety and product interaction was significant, the critical difference at the 5 per cent level being 0.28, with a coefficient of variation of 3.51 per cent.
478: Flavour integrates the perception of aroma and taste, and the most probable basis of the highest scores being obtained by the fortified treatments is that the gain in taste conferred by the added sugars outweighed the small loss of rice aroma occasioned by masking (Amerine et al., 1965; Meilgaard et al., 2007). The organic acids and volatile esters formed during lactic fermentation likewise contribute positively to the flavour of the product, and their concentration is conditioned by the fermentable substrate available in the batter, which the vegetable extract augments (Soni and Sandhu, 1990; Nout and Sarkar, 1999; Blandino et al., 2003; Ganzle, 2014). Kalojira scored highest, most probably because its own pigment and phenolic fraction confer a mild astringency perceived by the panel as depth of flavour, an effect reported for pigmented rice products by Sompong et al. (2011) and Pal et al. (2019).
487: Texture score (Table 4.39 and Fig. 4.39) differed significantly among the twelve treatment combinations. It was highest in KBI (8.14), followed by RBI (7.74), and lowest in DI (5.64). Among the products the mean value was 7.56 in the beet fortified product, 7.32 in the carrot fortified product and 6.49 in the plain product. Among the varieties it was highest in Kalojira (7.69) and lowest in Dudeshwar (6.52).
